tagline.text: A 300-year-old Earthquake Baroque masterpiece held up by massive buttresses

items.credit: Philip Nalangan / CC BY 4.0 / Wikimedia Commons

children.text: Completed around

, the Church of San Agustin is a masterpiece of Philippine Earthquake Baroque architecture, its 24 massive buttresses having withstood earthquakes for centuries. Inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in
, it sits just
30 minutes
from Laoag, making it a must-see stop on any Ilocos trip.
Paoay Church's official name is the Church of San Agustin. Augustinian friars began construction around
and completed it around
. In

it was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List together with the San Agustin Church in Intramuros, Manila, Miagao Church in Iloilo, and Santa Maria Church in Ilocos Sur, under the collective title "Baroque Churches of the Philippines." The Philippine government had already designated it a National Cultural Treasure earlier, in

What makes this church special is immediately visible: the massive buttresses along both sides. Twenty-four buttresses, several meters thick, lean against the walls on the sides and rear of the church, and it is considered the most dramatic example of the so-called "Earthquake Baroque" style, designed to keep buildings standing in earthquake-prone Philippines. It is said to have been built from coral stone and brick bound together with mortar mixed with lime and sugarcane juice, among other ingredients. The stepped gable at the top of the facade evokes the towers of Asian temples, giving the church a distinctive blend of Gothic, Baroque, and Oriental influences.
The freestanding three-story bell tower beside the church was completed in
. It is said that Katipunan revolutionaries used it as a watchtower during the

Philippine Revolution, and guerrillas did the same during World War II. It is especially beautiful at sunset, when the red brick glows gold, and at night during the Christmas season, when it is lit up.
It suits travelers who enjoy historic architecture and photography, as well as families touring Ilocos Norte from a base in Laoag. The church itself takes just
1–2 hours
to see, but Paoay Lake, Malacañang of the North, the Marcos Museum in Batac, and the Suba sand dunes are all nearby, making it easy to combine into a full-day itinerary.

Don't just view the facade and leave — walk slowly around the sides and back of the church. The row of buttresses with their scroll-shaped ornaments is the church's true face, and looking up from the shade between them gives you a real sense of scale.
Shooting wide-angle from the far end of the front lawn lets you fit the whole church and the bell tower into one frame. Mornings are backlit, so photos come out best after

The interior is more modest than the exterior, but the cool air created by the thick walls and the simple altar leave an impression. During Mass, watch quietly from the back, and on weekends, when weddings are frequent, it's polite to check the schedule before entering.

blocks.title: Examine the coral-stone walls by the bell tower

children.text: Get close and you can see the coral stone embedded between the bricks, the moss, and the weathering left by 300 years. Scratching the walls or climbing on them damages the heritage site and should be avoided.

Around the plaza are stalls selling Inabel, the traditional Ilocano woven fabric, along with local specialties like garlic, bagoong (fermented fish sauce), and chicharon. Inabel table runners or handkerchiefs make easy, affordable gifts.

blocks.title: Pinakbet pizza at the cafe across from the church

children.text: Herencia Café, across from the church, has long been known for its "pinakbet pizza," topped with the Ilocano vegetable dish pinakbet. It's a great spot for a late lunch with a view of the church.

blocks.title: Combine with Paoay Lake and Malacañang of the North

children.text: About
10 minutes

away by car, on the shore of Paoay Lake, Malacañang of the North — once a vacation home of the Marcos family — is now open to the public as a museum. Its breezy lakeview terrace makes it a pleasant stop after visiting the church.
The church's exterior is often lit up at night, and in
December
the plaza gets busy with Christmas decorations. Consider stopping by once more in the evening before heading back to your hotel in Laoag.

Several buses to Laoag depart daily from Cubao, Sampaloc, and other terminals in Manila, run by companies such as Partas, Fariñas Trans, and Maria de Leon. The trip takes about
9–11 hours

depending on regular or deluxe class. An overnight bus that departs at night and arrives in the morning is convenient. From Vigan, take a Laoag-bound bus and get off at the Batac or Paoay junction, about

Ilocos has one of the most distinct wet and dry seasons in the Philippines.
November
through
April
is the dry season, with little rain and clear skies that make for great photos of the red-brick church.
December–February
is cool and pleasant for walking, with morning and evening temperatures around 20°C, while from March to
May
midday temperatures climb close to 35°C, making the shadeless plaza quite hot.
From
June
through
October
, the southwest monsoon (habagat) brings frequent rain, and from July to
September
typhoons often pass through northern Luzon. Flights and buses to Laoag can be suspended when a typhoon hits, so it's wise to build extra time into your schedule during this period.
As for events, the feast of the church's patron saint, St. Augustine (around
August 28
), brings Mass and processions, and in
February
Laoag City holds the "Pamulinawen Festival" to mark its own patron saint's feast, packed with street parades and food stalls. Holy Week (the week before Easter) and
December
see a big rise in pilgrims and domestic travelers.

Paoay town has a few small guesthouses and resorts, but for more choice and easier transport, staying in Laoag city, about
30 minutes
away by car, is most convenient. Laoag has many clean, mid-range hotels priced around
per night, and the large Fort Ilocandia resort beside the sand dunes south of the city is popular with families. A few quiet resort-style lodgings can also be found on the shore of Paoay Lake.

Ilocano food is known for being salty and heavy on garlic. Must-tries include Batac empanada (an orange-hued fried dumpling of rice-flour dough filled with green papaya, egg, and longganisa), bagnet (crispy deep-fried pork belly), pinakbet (sautéed vegetables with bagnet), the tangy soup dinengdeng, and Ilocano-style longganisa sausage. Herencia Café in front of Paoay Church has long been famous among travelers for its pinakbet pizza and bagnet pizza, while Riverside Empanadaan, the empanada stall street in Batac, is a favorite with locals too.
Admission to the church is free, but interior viewing is limited during Mass and weddings. Weddings are common on weekend mornings and late afternoons, so weekday afternoons are quieter.
As it is a place of worship, avoid sleeveless tops and short shorts. Bring a light shirt or scarf to cover up if needed.
The best time for photos is
. The facade faces west, so the afternoon light turns the brick a warm red.
Paoay town has few ATMs, so withdraw enough cash in Laoag beforehand. Stalls and tricycles accept cash only.
When chartering a tricycle or van, agree on the list of stops, the total fare, and the waiting time before you set off, to avoid disputes later.
The plaza has almost no shade at midday. Bring a hat, sunscreen, and about a liter of water.
If combining this with a 4x4 tour of the Suba sand dunes, visit the church first and head to the dunes late in the afternoon to avoid the hottest sand.
If you're also visiting Vigan, Paoay lies right along the Vigan–Laoag route, so it's efficient to stop by on the way.
The church is a cultural treasure over 300 years old. Climbing the buttresses, prying off bricks, or flying a drone without permission is prohibited and may be penalized.
During restoration or repair work, some areas may be covered with scaffolding or closed off. Check announcements from Paoay Church or the Ilocos Norte tourism office before visiting.
There is a risk of heatstroke at midday from March to
May
. Drink water often, especially if combining this with a visit to the sand dunes.
During typhoon season from July to
September
, flights and buses are often canceled and coastal roads can flood. Check PAGASA forecasts and build a spare day into your schedule.
If someone around the plaza offers to "guide" you, confirm the fee up front, and feel free to politely decline if you don't want the service.
The church is a living place of worship where Mass is still held today. Please remember it is a place of prayer first, and a tourist attraction second.
